questions.q: What does an OAuth-secured integration send on each outbound request, instead of a reusable username and password?
options: A short-lived access token obtained by exchanging a client ID and client secret
The client secret itself, base64-encoded
A permanent API key that never expires
A digital certificate issued by the external server
questions.explain: OAuth exchanges a client ID and secret for a short-lived access token, and that token — not the underlying secret — travels on each call.

questions.q: What does an OAuth Entity Profile actually do in a ServiceNow integration?
options: It stores the raw username and password for Basic Auth
It points at an OAuth Entity record and selects which grant type to use, and is what gets attached to a REST Message's Authentication Profile
It replaces the need for a REST Message entirely
It is only used for inbound, not outbound, integrations
questions.explain: The OAuth Entity Profile is the piece attached to the Authentication Profile; it references an OAuth Entity record (client ID/secret/token endpoint) and the chosen grant type.

questions.q: A nightly, unattended job pulls data from a partner API with no human user involved. Which OAuth grant type fits, and why?
options: Authorization Code, because every integration should involve user consent
Basic Auth, because grant types only apply to inbound integrations
Authorization Code, because it never expires
Client Credentials, because the integration authenticates as itself using only its client ID and client secret, with no human user in the flow
questions.explain: Client Credentials is the standard grant for server-to-server integrations where no human is present to authorize anything.

questions.q: When should the Authorization Code grant be used instead of Client Credentials?
options: Whenever the external API's token endpoint URL is unknown
Whenever a shorter access token lifetime is preferred
Whenever the integration needs to act on behalf of a specific human user who has explicitly authorized that access
Whenever the integration should authenticate as itself with no user involved
questions.explain: Authorization Code represents a specific user's own consent and permissions; Client Credentials represents the integration's own identity with no user involved.

questions.q: Once an OAuth Entity Profile is configured on a REST Message's Authentication Profile, what does the developer's script no longer need to manage directly?
options: Requesting, caching, and refreshing the access token — ServiceNow handles that automatically
The REST Message's target URL
Whether the request uses REST or SOAP
The name of the Authentication Profile
questions.explain: That's the real practical benefit this lesson highlights: ServiceNow's OAuth support removes manual token-lifecycle management from the integration's script entirely.
